newsitem.title: JAPAN: Mondale says N.Korea sub won't affect nuclear pact.
newsitem.headline: Mondale says N.Korea sub won't affect nuclear pact.

text.p: U.S. ambassador to Japan Walter Mondale said on Wednesday that a recent submarine incident would not affect the nuclear agreement between Washington and Pyongyang.
"There are still major tensions and uncertainties on the Korean Peninsula, as the recent submarine incident reminds us," Mondale told a Tokyo seminar.
"But the (nuclear) agreement with Pyongyang is working. We are on a much better footing," he added.
On Tuesday, North Korea issued a veiled warning to the United States that their landmark 1994 nuclear agreement could be jeopardised by Washington's stand on the submarine incident.
Seoul said last month that a submarine had landed 26 North Koreans on an east coast beach of South Korea. One of them was captured and 22 killed. The others are believed to be still at large.

South Korea said they were on an infiltration mission, while North Korea said the submarine ran aground after suffering engine trouble. The two Koreas have remained technically at war since the 1950-53 Korean conflict.

In Seoul last week, U.S. Assistant Secretary of State Winston Lord said Washington and Seoul would press ahead with the agreement, under which Pyongyang pledged to freeze a possible nuclear weapons programme in return for two nuclear reactors financed largely by South Korea.
But without referring directly to the submarine incident, he told a news conference there would be "a pause in the pace of our activities".
Seoul, which had pledged to foot most of the $5 billion cost of building nuclear plants for the communist state, hinted it might withdraw its backing for the nuclear accord.
On Tuesday, the U.N. Security Council expressed serious concern over the submarine incident and called for strict observance of the armistice agreement.

In its first statement since 1953 on the Korean armistice, the council said that "the Korean Armistice Agreement should be fully observed and that no action should be taken that might increase tension or undermine peace and stability on the Korean peninsula".
"Fortunately the Asia-Pacific region is now stable, but the future poses many uncertainties. As I noted, the Korean Peninsula remains divided and dangerous," Mondale said on Wednesday.
